title: Constant-factor related-machine precedence scheduling
formal: Does nonpreemptive precedence-constrained makespan minimization on uniformly related parallel machines admit a deterministic polynomial-time approximation with a universal constant factor? Precisely, do there exist one algorithm \(A\), constants \(K\ge1,C>0\), and an integer \(b\ge1\), such that for every instance of binary encoding length \(L\) specified below, \(A\) returns a feasible schedule of makespan at most \(K\,\mathrm{OPT}\) in at most \(C(L+1)^b\) Turing-machine steps? All constants are independent of the numbers of jobs and machines, processing requirements, machine speeds and precedence graph.
why: Identical machines already allow nontrivial parallelism constrained by a dependency graph, and different speeds add a global allocation choice. A universal constant approximation would show that this extra heterogeneity can be handled with bounded worst-case loss. A negative resolution would identify a basic source of approximation difficulty even though every job can run on every machine and execution times have the simple requirement-divided-by-speed form.
status_note: Explicitly highlighted in the 2011 book. The checked later upper bound is Li’s nonconstant approximation, and the checked 2022 inapproximability result for this exact model depends on additional unproved assumptions. The 2023 communication-aware result and bounded 2025–2026 searches through 2026-09-15 did not yield a constant approximation or an unconditional refutation of its existence. This review does not certify an exhaustive literature search.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-15; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: The Design of Approximation Algorithms, Problem 8, highlights the absence of a constant approximation for related machines with precedence constraints, while recording an O(log m) upper bound.
Li’s Theorem 1.3 gives an \(O(\log m/\log\log m)\) approximation for both precedence-constrained makespan and total weighted completion time on related machines; Section 4 proves the makespan bound.
Davies et al. publish conditional related-machine hardness in SODA 2022. Theorem 4.1 requires their Conjecture 1.2 and the assumption that NP has no quasipolynomial-time algorithms.

Su et al. publish communication-aware guarantees in Operations Research Letters. The corresponding zero-communication specialization retains a growing logarithmic-over-iterated-logarithmic approximation factor.

category_assignment.reason: Topic of the imported textbook or survey question

importance.reason: A central long-standing approximation question at the boundary between identical and arbitrary machine environments. It asks whether speed heterogeneity and precedence alone force a growing loss, connecting a canonical scheduling model to substantial structural inapproximability conjectures rather than tuning an isolated ratio.

sentences: The problem asks for a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation to the makespan of precedence-constrained jobs on machines with different speeds.
Every job may use every machine, and its uninterrupted execution time is its processing requirement divided by the selected machine’s speed.
The approximation factor must remain fixed as the number of machines and the range of speeds grow.
The checked general upper bound grows logarithmically divided by an iterated logarithm, while known stronger hardness uses extra unproved hypotheses.
A solution must cover arbitrary finite rational inputs in the explicitly stated deterministic bit model.

definitions: An instance consists of integers \(n,m\ge1\), jobs \(J=[n]\), machines \(M=[m]\), positive rational job requirements \(p_j\), positive rational machine speeds \(s_i\), and a directed acyclic graph \(D=(J,E)\) of precedence requirements. Write \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). A job \(j\) assigned to machine \(a(j)\in M\) occupies one uninterrupted interval \([t_j,t_j+p_j/s_{a(j)})\), with start \(t_j\ge0\). Two intervals on the same machine must be disjoint, and every edge \((j,\ell)\in E\) imposes \(t_\ell\ge t_j+p_j/s_{a(j)}\). Every job executes exactly once on exactly one machine; it cannot be split, migrated or duplicated. Every job is eligible on every machine, and all jobs and the entire precedence graph are supplied before scheduling. There are no communication delays, release times, job weights or additional restrictions. The makespan is \(C_{\max}(a,t)=\max_{j\in J}(t_j+p_j/s_{a(j)})\). Define \(\mathrm{OPT}\) as the infimum of this makespan over all feasible assignments and nonnegative real start times; it is finite and positive. The input explicitly lists \(n,m\), the graph’s edge pairs, and each positive rational as a binary positive numerator and denominator in lowest terms. Counts and edge endpoints are binary integers with fixed separators; \(L\) is the total bit length of this list. No bound on numerical magnitudes or speed ratios is imposed beyond this finite encoding. The output explicitly lists each machine assignment and a nonnegative rational start time, again in binary rational form. The algorithm is one finite deterministic program with ordinary work tapes, and its time includes parsing, exact arithmetic and writing the complete output. Polynomial dependence on the numerical values rather than their bit lengths does not qualify. Randomized or expected-only guarantees are outside this stated deterministic target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the stated universal constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm exists, or prove the negation of that existence statement. An affirmative answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove feasibility, the multiplicative makespan guarantee and the polynomial bit-complexity bound for every input. A negative answer must exclude every finite universal factor and every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. A theorem conditional on an additional unproved scheduling or complexity hypothesis does not establish that unconditional negation. Bounds growing with \(m\), algorithms restricted to a fixed number of machines or speed values, and results for a different scheduling objective do not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Williamson and Shmoys list this as Problem 8 among the book’s highlighted open approximation questions. The surrounding discussion contrasts the constant guarantee for identical machines with the then-known logarithmic guarantee when speeds vary. The target remains existence of a constant approximation, with the ordinary deterministic finite-input model made explicit.

Shi Li’s Theorem 1.3 improves the general upper bound to \(O(\log m/\log\log m)\) as \(m\) grows; the guarantee can be written \(O(1+\log(m+2)/\log\log(m+3))\) to include small \(m\). Although the paper title emphasizes total weighted completion time, its theorem explicitly covers makespan as well. The 2011 book’s logarithmic bound is therefore historical rather than the latest checked upper bound.

Bazzi and Norouzi-Fard obtain nonconstant hardness under an additional structural hypothesis about multipartite graphs. Davies and coauthors subsequently derive a growing lower bound for related-machine precedence scheduling from their Unique Machine Precedence Scheduling conjecture together with the exclusion of quasipolynomial algorithms for NP. Those assumptions remain part of the cited results.

The unconditional reduction in the latter work is often encountered under a title about communication delays. Its main communication-delay hardness result concerns a different model; its consequence for the delay-free related-machine problem here still requires the additional scheduling conjecture. Neither consequence is recorded as an unconditional resolution of this card.

Su, Ren, Vardi and Wierman study related machines with machine-dependent communication effects. Their bound also refers to a communication-free optimum, and specializes to a nonconstant approximation when the extra communication contribution vanishes. It does not supply a universal constant for arbitrary speed ratios.
